'''Landon Rabern''' (1981–2020) was an American mathematician and computer scientist, best known for his contributions to [[graph theory]], logic, and [[artificial intelligence]].<ref name="rabern2023">{{cite journal |last=Rabern |first=Brian |author2=Cranston, D. W. |author3=Kierstead, H. |title=Special issue in honour of Landon Rabern |journal=Discrete Mathematics |publisher=Elsevier |year=2023|volume=346 |issue=11 |article-number=113507 |doi=10.1016/j.disc.2023.113507 }}</ref><ref name=":0" />

His research primarily focused on problems related to graph coloring, including work on [[Brooks' theorem]], the Borodin–[[Alexandr Kostochka|Kostochka]] conjecture, list critical graphs, and [[Reed's conjecture]]. Rabern earned a Ph.D. in mathematics from Arizona State University in 2013, under the supervision of Hal Kierstead,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=176173|title=Landon Rabern - The Mathematics Genealogy Project|website=www.mathgenealogy.org}}</ref> with a dissertation that explored coloring graphs using nearly maximum-degree-sized palettes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://hdl.handle.net/2286/R.I.17753 |title=Landon Rabern's Dissertation |website=Arizona State University Digital Repository |hdl=2286/R.I.17753 |access-date=22 January 2025}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Rabern was born and raised in [[Roseburg, Oregon]]. He developed an early interest in computers, and machine intelligence. In the 1980s, he began programming on a Commodore 64, learning languages such as [[BASIC]], [[Pascal (programming language)]], and [[C (programming language)]]. By high school, he had created a chess AI, known as "Betsy,"<ref>[https://www.chessprogramming.org/Betsy "Betsy"], Chess Programming Wiki.</ref> which is credited as the first published chess engine capable of playing [[Fisher Random Chess]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chessprogramming.org/Landon_Rabern |title=Landon Rabern |website=ChessProgramming.org |access-date=22 January 2025}}</ref>

Rabern pursued studies in mathematics and computer science at Washington University in St. Louis, with a year abroad in the Netherlands. He later earned a master's degree in mathematics from the University of California, Santa Barbara. While working as a software engineer, Rabern continued to independently explore graph theory. His proof of a conjecture in the field led him to pursue a Ph.D. at Arizona State University.

== Career and research ==
Rabern made significant contributions to graph theory, particularly in areas such as the Borodin–Kostochka conjecture, list critical graphs, and Reed's conjecture.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Cranston | first1 = Daniel W. | last2 = Rabern | first2 = Landon | title = Planar graphs are 9/2-colorable | journal = Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B | volume = 133 | pages = 32–45 | year = 2018 | doi = 10.1016/j.jctb.2018.04.002 | url = https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2018.04.002 | arxiv = 1410.7233 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last = Rabern
| first = Landon
| title = Δ-Critical graphs with small high vertex cliques
| journal = Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B
| volume = 102
| issue = 1
| pages = 126–130
| year = 2012
| doi = 10.1016/j.jctb.2011.05.003
| url = https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2011.05.003
| arxiv = 1102.1023
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Kierstead
| first1 = H. A.
| last2 = Rabern
| first2 = Landon
| title = Improved lower bounds on the number of edges in list critical and online list critical graphs
| journal = Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B
| volume = 140
| pages = 147–170
| year = 2020
| doi = 10.1016/j.jctb.2019.05.004
| url = https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2019.05.004
| arxiv = 1406.7355
}}</ref> His work in discrete mathematics and combinatorics was recognized for its rigor and creativity.<ref name="rabern2023" /><ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=American Mathematical Society News: Landon Rabern's Contributions |url=https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=6655 |website=American Mathematical Society |access-date=22 January 2025}}</ref> Rabern's work extended beyond mathematics into computer science and philosophy. Notably, he explored the use of automated theorem proving and computer-assisted proofs in graph theory. He also made contributions to the study of semantic paradoxes (e.g., [[Yablo's paradox]]) by applying graph-theoretic methods.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rabern |first1=Landon |last2=Rabern |first2=Brian |last3=Macauley |first3=Matthew |title=Dangerous Reference Graphs and Semantic Paradoxes |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=42 |issue=5 |pages=727–765 |year=2013 |doi=10.1007/s10992-012-9245-6|doi-broken-date=1 July 2025 }}</ref><ref>Bolander, Thomas, "Self-Reference and Paradox", ''The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy'' (Fall 2024 Edition), Edward N. Zalta & Uri Nodelman (eds.), https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2024/entries/self-reference/</ref><ref>Beringer, T., & Schindler, T. (2017). "A graph-theoretic analysis of the semantic paradoxes". ''Bulletin of Symbolic Logic'', 23(4), 442–492.</ref> And in another article provided a novel (two-question) solution to "[[The Hardest Logic Puzzle Ever]]".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rabern |first1=Brian |last2=Rabern |first2=Landon |title=A simple solution to the hardest logic puzzle ever |journal=Analysis |volume=68 |issue=2 |pages=105–112 |year=2008 |doi=10.1093/analys/68.2.105}}</ref><ref>Uzquiano, G. (2010). "How to solve the hardest logic puzzle ever in two questions". ''Analysis'', 70(1), 39–44.</ref> He also contributed a satirical mathematical proof titled ''"A Teleological Argument"'' for the existence of the [[Flying Spaghetti Monster]], published in ''[[The Gospel of the Flying Spaghetti Monster]]''.<ref>Henderson, Bobby. ''The Gospel of the Flying Spaghetti Monster''. Random House Inc, 2006.</ref>

In addition to his academic research, Rabern had a successful career in [[software engineering]] and [[data science]], co-founding a software company and working with several technology firms, particularly those focused on artificial intelligence and social media. In the final years of his career, Rabern returned to his early interest in artificial intelligence and chess programming. He began a second Ph.D. in Cognitive Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where he focused on the intersection of psychology and machine learning. Rabern died in 2020 at the age of 39.<ref>{{cite web |title=Landon Wade Rabern |url=https://www.nrtoday.com/obits/landon-wade-rabern/article_0634b8a7-4424-5787-bde0-64d99dfe93c4.html |website=The News-Review |date=22 October 2020 |access-date=22 January 2025}}</ref>
